latvian gambit.intro: We're playing the white side of the Latvian Gambit, a sharp and unsound opening where Black pushes the f-pawn early, weakening their kingside. Our plan is to open the center and exploit the exposed king with simple, forceful moves.
latvian gambit.shortIntro: White punishes Black's early f5 with central play and direct threats.
latvian gambit.outro: By opening the center and targeting the weak f7 square, we've built a winning attack. Simple development and concrete tactics are all it takes to refute the Latvian Gambit.

ideas.text: e4 opens the game, claiming central space and freeing your bishop and queen. It's the standard first move, setting the stage for active play.
e5 is Black's natural reply, mirroring your central pawn. The game is now in classic open-game territory.
Nf3 develops the knight to its best square, attacking e5 and preparing to castle. This is the most common and principled move.
f5 is the Latvian Gambit, a dubious move that weakens Black's kingside and opens diagonals. Black hopes to surprise you, but we'll punish it by opening the center with d4.
Bc4 develops the bishop to a powerful diagonal, eyeing f7—the weakest square in Black's camp. This move increases pressure and threatens immediate checkmate if Black isn't careful.
fxe4 captures your e4 pawn, but Black's king is now even more exposed. Instead of recapturing automatically, we look for a more forceful continuation.
Nxe5 sacrifices the knight temporarily, but it opens the e5 square for your queen. This is a classic idea: trade on e5 to deliver a devastating check on h5.
Qg5 is Black's attempt to defend f7 and counterattack, but it leaves the queen misplaced. We now have a powerful follow-up: Nf7 forks the queen and rook.
Nf7 forks Black's queen and rook, winning material. This knight jump is the direct punishment for Black's careless play—the queen must move, and we'll capture the rook.

Qxg2 — Black ignores the fork, snapping off a pawn and attacking the rook on h1. It looks scary, but the queen has wandered far from her own king, and your fork on f7 still wins the exchange. Defend calmly and the counterplay evaporates.
ideas.shortText: Qxg2 ignores the fork and attacks the rook on h1.

ideas.text: Rf1 is a quiet but essential move. It gets the rook off the back rank and prepares to join the attack, while also defending the f2 pawn. Black's king is still exposed, and we want to bring all our pieces into the game.
ideas.shortText: Rf1 brings the rook into play.

ideas.text: d5 is a desperate attempt by Black to block the diagonal and gain space. But it doesn't solve the king's safety issues. We can simply continue our development, as Black's position remains full of holes.
Nxh8 collects the cornered rook. The knight may take a few moves to find its way out of h8, but the material is decisive and Black's king remains the one in real danger.
ideas.shortText: Nxh8 collects the rook in the corner.

ideas.text: Nf6 is a final blunder, but the game is already lost. Black's knight moves to f6, but it doesn't defend anything crucial. We can now finish with a simple tactic, like Qe2+ followed by Rd1, winning the queen.

four knights game glek system.intro: Welcome to the Four Knights Game: Glek System. This is an underrated weapon that sets up a fianchetto against Black's king pawn setup. Let's walk through the first critical moves.
four knights game glek system.shortIntro: Glek System: fianchetto the bishop to fight for the center.
four knights game glek system.outro: After Nxd5, Black has central control but White's fianchettoed bishop and flexible setup offer dynamic chances. The key ideas are to complete kingside development and prepare either d4 or f4 breaks.

ideas.text: e4 opens the center and stakes a claim in the heart of the board. This is the standard first move for White, aiming to control d5 and f5.
e5 is Black's symmetrical response, also grabbing central space and freeing the f8 bishop.
Nf3 develops a knight to its best square, attacking e5 and preparing to castle kingside.
Nc6 develops Black's knight, defending e5 and eyeing d4.
Nc3 develops the other knight, supporting e4 and preparing to challenge the center.
Nf6 develops Black's knight, attacking e4 and putting pressure on White's center.

g3 is the hallmark of the Glek System. You fianchetto the bishop to g2, controlling the long diagonal and preparing to castle. This move often catches Black off guard because it's less common than d4 or Bb5.
d5 is Black's principled central strike, challenging White's e4 pawn and opening lines. This is the most common and critical response to g3.
exd5 captures the pawn, opening the center and forcing Black to recapture. White is not afraid of the resulting pawn structure.

Nxd5 recaptures with the knight, centralizing it and threatening to disrupt White's pawns if Black takes on c3. This is a key moment: Black's knight on d5 is active, but White's fianchettoed bishop will target it.
Bg2. We fianchetto our bishop, completing our kingside development. This bishop will be a key defender and attacker along the long diagonal, especially after the center opens.
ideas.shortText: Bg2 fianchettoes the bishop, controlling the long diagonal.

ideas.text: Nxc3. Black trades knights, capturing on c3. This is a common decision in the Glek; we should be happy to recapture with the b-pawn, as it opens the b-file and prepares d2-d4.
ideas.shortText: Nxc3 trades knights, leading to doubled pawns for us.

ideas.text: bxc3. We recapture with the b-pawn, accepting doubled pawns. This structure is intentional: it opens the b-file for our rook and makes it easier to push d4, gaining central control. The doubled pawns are not a weakness here—they give us dynamic play.
ideas.shortText: bxc3 opens the b-file and prepares d4.

elephant gambit.intro: We're playing the white side of the Elephant Gambit. Black's second move d5 is a sharp gambit, but we can handle it with precise play. Let's walk through the critical line.
elephant gambit.shortIntro: White's response to the Elephant Gambit.
elephant gambit.outro: With Qg5, Black's queen enters the game early. We have a strong position with better development and central control. Stay alert for tactics.

ideas.text: We start with e4, claiming the center and opening lines for our pieces. This is the foundation of our opening play.
Black plays e5, mirroring our central pawn. This is a standard response, but now we can develop our knight.
We develop the knight to f3, attacking the e5 pawn and preparing to castle. This is a natural developing move.
Black plays d5, the Elephant Gambit. They sacrifice a pawn to gain quick development and disrupt our center. We need to be precise.
Nxe5 accepts the gambit — we grab the pawn and our knight lands on a strong central square. Precision from here keeps the extra material.
Black recaptures with dxe4, attacking our knight. This is a natural follow-up, but we have a strong response.
We develop the bishop to c4, eyeing the f7 square and preparing to castle. This puts immediate pressure on Black's weak f7 pawn.
Black plays Qg5, attacking our knight and threatening the g2 pawn. This is a tricky move, but we can handle it by developing further or moving the knight. Our position remains solid.

sicilian defense grand prix attack.intro: We're playing the Grand Prix Attack — White's ferocious answer to the Sicilian, and the whole story aims at one square: f7. We'll brace the centre, launch the f-pawn, point the bishop at f7 and swing the queen toward h4, ripping open the f-file before Black's queenside counterplay ever arrives. Watch how every move feeds that single plan.
sicilian defense grand prix attack.shortIntro: The Grand Prix: White's kingside storm aimed at f7.
sicilian defense grand prix attack.outro: With f4, White has committed to the Grand Prix structure — the bishop will go to c4, the queen will eye h4, and the attack on f7 begins. Black now needs to choose a setup: fianchetto with g6, or play e6/d6 to keep the center solid. The battle lines are drawn.

ideas.text: e4 opens the game and stakes a claim in the center — the first step in any aggressive Sicilian setup. White immediately signals that this won't be a quiet positional game.
ideas.shortText: e4 claims central space and starts the fight.

ideas.text: c5 is Black's classic Sicilian response, immediately challenging White's center from the flank. It prevents White from building a big pawn duo with d4 and sets up an asymmetrical struggle where Black will counterattack on the queenside or in the center.
ideas.shortText: c5 challenges the center and starts Sicilian counterplay.

ideas.text: Nc3 does double duty: it defends e4 so Black can't strike there for free, and it keeps the knight off f3 for now, letting White decide which attacking setup to build. This is the hallmark of the Grand Prix — White delays d4 to avoid opening lines for Black's pieces.
ideas.shortText: Nc3 defends e4 and keeps options open.

ideas.text: Nc6 is Black's most flexible move here — it develops a piece without committing to a specific pawn structure. Black waits to see where White puts the bishop before deciding whether to play d6, e6, or g6. This keeps Black ready to respond to White's plan.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 develops and waits for White's bishop.

ideas.text: f4 is the defining move of the Grand Prix Attack. White immediately starts building a kingside pawn storm, planning to follow up with Bc4 (or Bb5) and Qe1-h4. The idea is to rip open the f-file and deliver checkmate before Black can organize counterplay. Black must now choose a solid setup — the most common are g6 (fianchetto) or e6/d6 (classical).
ideas.shortText: f4 launches the kingside attack; Black must respond carefully.

sicilian defense grand prix attack.shortIntroFlipped: White launches a kingside pawn storm; we must choose a setup to neutralize it.
sicilian defense grand prix attack.outroFlipped: With a flexible setup and careful development, we've sidestepped White's immediate threats and can now focus on our own counterplay in the center or queenside.

bird opening.intro: Welcome to the Bird Opening. White starts with a flank pawn push, aiming to control e5 and develop quickly. Black responds by occupying the center with d5, a solid reply.
bird opening.shortIntro: Bird Opening: f4, d5, Nf3, g6, g3, Bg7, Bg2, Nf6, O-O, O-O.
bird opening.outro: Both sides have castled, reaching a typical position from the Bird Opening. White has a flexible setup with the fianchettoed bishop, while Black has solid development. The game is balanced, with plans involving central breaks like e5 or c5.

ideas.text: f4: White starts with the Bird Opening, a flank attack that aims to control e5 and create kingside pressure. This move avoids mainline theory and can lead to unique positions.
d5: Black stakes a claim in the center, challenging White's control. This is the most principled response, occupying d5 and preparing development.
Nf3: White develops the knight to f3, supporting the e5 square and preparing kingside castling. It also prevents Black from playing e5 easily.
g6: Black fianchettoes the kingside bishop, preparing to put it on g7 to pressure the long diagonal. This is a flexible setup, often leading to a King's Indian or Grünfeld-like structure.
g3: White mirrors Black's fianchetto, developing the bishop to g2. This solidifies the kingside and eyes the center.
Bg7: Black completes the fianchetto, placing the bishop on g7. It targets the d4 square and supports potential central breaks.
Bg2: White's bishop settles on g2, aiming at the center and the queenside. It's a key piece in the Bird's setup.
Nf6: Black develops the knight to f6, preparing to castle and increasing control over e4. It also eyes the kingside.
O-O: White castles kingside, bringing the king to safety and connecting the rooks. This is a natural move in the Bird Opening.
O-O: Black also castles kingside, completing development and ensuring king safety. Both sides are now ready for the middlegame.
d3 keeps the centre stable, taking e4 away from Black's pieces and freeing the c1-bishop's diagonal. A quiet move that finishes the setup before the queenside plans begin.
ideas.shortText: d3 restrains e4 and frees the c1-bishop.

ideas.text: c5 stakes out queenside space and eyes d4. Black wants to expand on that wing, so keep your centre firm and your pieces coordinated.
c3 guards the d4 square and blunts the g7-bishop's long diagonal. With the centre held, you can develop the queenside knight at your own pace.
ideas.shortText: c3 guards d4, blunts the long diagonal.

ideas.text: Nc6: Black develops the knight, eyeing the d4 square and supporting the c5 pawn. You'll need to find a good square for your own knight.
Na3: You develop the knight to the edge, planning to reroute it to c2 where it can support the center and potentially jump to e3 or b4.
Rb8: Black prepares to push b5, gaining space on the queenside. You should anticipate this and keep your pieces coordinated.
Nc2: Your knight reaches its ideal square, eyeing b4 and e3. It also frees the a3 square for the rook if needed.
b5: Black expands on the queenside, but this weakens the c5 pawn. You can now consider targeting it with moves like a4 or preparing to open the center.

sicilian defense taimanov variation.intro: We're stepping into the Sicilian Taimanov, a flexible and solid system for Black. The key ideas are controlling the center with e6 and developing harmoniously, aiming for a strong pawn structure and active piece play.
sicilian defense taimanov variation.shortIntro: Sicilian Taimanov: solid, flexible, and ready to counterattack.
sicilian defense taimanov variation.outro: That's the Taimanov setup. Black has a solid structure and good development, ready for a strategic middlegame.

ideas.text: e4 opens the center and grabs space. White's first move claims the center and prepares to develop the king's pieces.
c5 is the Sicilian response, immediately challenging White's central pawn and creating an asymmetrical pawn structure that leads to dynamic play.
Nf3 develops the knight to a natural square, supporting the d4 push and putting pressure on Black's c5 pawn.
e6 is the hallmark of the Taimanov. It prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop and reinforces the d5 square, keeping the center flexible.
ideas.shortText: e6 prepares development and controls d5.

ideas.text: d4 is White's central break, aiming to open lines and gain space. Black's response will determine the pawn structure.
ideas.shortText: d4 opens the center for White.

ideas.text: cxd4 accepts the pawn exchange, simplifying the center and opening the c-file for Black's rook. This is the standard Taimanov capture.
ideas.shortText: cxd4 opens the c-file for Black.

ideas.text: Nxd4 recaptures with the knight, centralizing it and maintaining pressure. The knight on d4 is well-placed but can be a target.
Nc6 develops the knight and attacks White's knight on d4. This is a natural developing move that also challenges White's central outpost.

Nb5.text: You know this road well — everything up to here is the Taimanov you've already mastered. The main line plays Nc3, keeping the center solid and preparing the familiar dance where your queen comes to c7 and Ndb5 knocks it back. Today's sideline, Nb5, is a different beast: the knight jumps in eyeing the d6 square, and you calmly take that square away with d6. White grabs space with c4, and only after a6 does the knight concede the trip to a3, where it sits on the rim. That wandering costs time — you develop freely and castle, and the fight becomes piece activity against White's space rather than the usual central tension.
Nb5.shortText: Nc3 is the main road; Nb5 eyes d6 — blunt it, then a6 sends it to a3.
Nb5.textFlipped: You know this road well — everything up to here is the Taimanov you've already mastered. The main line plays Nc3, keeping the center solid and preparing the familiar dance where Black's queen comes to c7 and Ndb5 knocks it back. Today's sideline, Nb5, is a different beast: we jump in eyeing the d6 square, Black blunts it with d6, and we grab space with c4. After a6 our knight concedes the trip to a3 — the price of the early jump — so the plan shifts: lean on the extra space, regroup the rim knight, and squeeze a slow maneuvering game instead of the usual central battle.
Nb5.shortTextFlipped: Nc3 is the main road; with Nb5 we trade knight time for c4 space.

rubinstein opening.intro: We're playing the Rubinstein Opening, a solid and flexible system. The key is to build a strong pawn center and develop pieces harmoniously, preparing for a kingside attack.
rubinstein opening.shortIntro: Rubinstein Opening: build center, develop, attack.
rubinstein opening.outro: With this setup, we've established a firm grip on the center and good piece coordination. Now we can look to castle and continue with our plans, keeping an eye on Black's counterplay.

ideas.text: We start with d4, claiming the center and opening lines for our pieces. This is the foundation of our opening system.
Black plays Nf6, developing and attacking our pawn. We're not worried; we'll continue with our setup.
Nf3 develops our knight, supporting the d4 pawn and preparing to bring out the bishop. Simple and solid.
Black plays e6, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop and reinforcing the center. We continue with our plan.
e3 is a flexible move, solidifying our pawn chain and opening a diagonal for our light-squared bishop. It's a key part of our setup.
Black plays c5, challenging our center. We'll maintain our structure and develop our bishop next.
Bd3 develops the bishop to a strong diagonal, eyeing the kingside. This is a typical square in our system.

Black develops Nc6, putting pressure on our center. We'll finish our development with Bb2 next.

Castling kingside is a natural and safe move here. It tucks your king away and brings your rook into the game, ready to support the center or join an attack. With your pieces well-placed, this is the perfect moment to secure your king's safety.
ideas.shortText: Castle to safety and activate your rook.

ideas.text: Black develops the bishop to d6, eyeing the kingside and the e5 square. This is a solid developing move, but it also signals that Black might be looking to push e5 or create threats on the long diagonal. Keep an eye on that bishop—it's well-placed for Black's plans.

Now we fianchetto our own bishop to b2. This is a key part of our setup—it controls the long diagonal, pressures the center, and supports any future pawn breaks like e4 or f4. With the bishop here, our position becomes very harmonious.
ideas.shortText: Fianchetto the bishop to control the diagonal.

ideas.text: Black castles kingside as well, completing their development. Both sides are now ready for the middlegame. Our setup is solid: we have a safe king, active pieces, and clear plans. The fight for the center and potential kingside expansion will decide the game.

queen s pawn game colle system.intro: This is the Colle System, a setup where White builds a solid, harmonious position before striking in the center. The whole line revolves around the fight for the e5 square — White wants to control it with pieces and pawns, while Black tries to challenge it. Every move here is about supporting that central idea.
queen s pawn game colle system.shortIntro: The Colle System: White builds a solid center to fight for e5.
queen s pawn game colle system.outro: With both kings castled, the stage is set. White's pieces are perfectly placed to support the e4 break or a kingside attack, while Black's setup is solid but passive. The battle for the center and the initiative is just beginning.

ideasFlipped.text: c6 shores up our center, making it harder for White to break through with e4. This is a solid, flexible move that also gives our queen a potential square on c7. We're reinforcing our position and preparing to counterattack if White overextends.
ideasFlipped.shortText: c6 reinforces our center.

ideasFlipped.text: Nbd2 is White's final piece of setup. The knight supports e4 and keeps their center solid, while their pieces are all harmoniously placed. Now it's our turn to find a plan. We have a solid position, and we can start thinking about how to create counterplay.
ideasFlipped.shortText: Nbd2 completes White's development.

polish opening king s indian variation s.openingName: Polish Opening: King's Indian Variation, Sokolsky Attack
polish opening king s indian variation s.intro: We're playing the Polish Opening, aiming to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and control the center. Black responds with King's Indian setup, and we'll look to build a solid pawn structure while keeping the bishop active.
polish opening king s indian variation s.shortIntro: Polish Opening: fianchetto and central control.
polish opening king s indian variation s.outro: We've reached a solid position with our bishop on b2 and flexible pawns. Black has castled, and we can now consider pushing d4 to challenge the center.

ideas.text: b4 starts the Polish Opening, immediately staking a claim on the queenside. It's an unusual move that aims to fianchetto the bishop and control the c5 square, often catching opponents off guard.
ideas.shortText: b4 starts the Polish Opening, claiming queenside space.

ideas.text: Nf6 develops the knight to a natural square, attacking nothing yet but preparing to challenge the center. Black's knight is well-placed here, eyeing the e4 and g4 squares.
Bb2 completes the fianchetto, putting pressure on the center and the g7 square. The bishop is well-placed here, eyeing the long diagonal.
g6 signals Black's intention to fianchetto their own bishop, leading to a King's Indian setup. This is a solid response, but we can continue with our own development.
c4 strengthens our control over the center and supports the b4 pawn. It also prepares to develop the knight to c3, though we should be mindful of potential d4 from Black.
ideas.shortText: c4 strengthens the center and supports b4.

ideas.text: Bg7 completes Black's fianchetto, putting their bishop on the long diagonal. This is standard in the King's Indian, and we need to be careful not to let them dominate the center.
e3 is a solid move that reinforces the d4 square and prepares to develop the kingside. It also prevents any immediate threats to our pawn structure.
ideas.shortText: e3 solidifies the center and prepares development.

ideas.text: Black plays d6, solidifying the center and preparing to develop the kingside. This is a standard King's Indian setup, keeping options open for future pawn breaks.
ideas.shortText: d6 solidifies the center and prepares kingside development.

ideas.text: Nf3 develops the knight to a natural square, supporting the d4 push and preparing to castle. The knight eyes e5 and g5, typical squares in this setup.
O-O castles Black's king to safety, a standard move in the King's Indian. Now we can consider our own plans, such as pushing d4 to challenge the center.

d4 completes the broad centre — pawns on b4, c4 and d4 grab space across the board, with the b2-bishop waiting behind them for the long diagonal to open. From here the plan is simple: finish development, castle, and expand on the queenside where the space is already yours.

queen s pawn game stonewall attack.intro: We're setting up the Stonewall Attack, a solid and aggressive system for White. The key is to build a strong pawn center and launch a kingside attack.
queen s pawn game stonewall attack.outro: With the bishop on d3, our Stonewall is nearly complete. Next we'll bring the knight to f3 and prepare to anchor it on e5.

ideas.text: d4 claims the center and opens lines for the queen and bishop. This is the foundation of the Stonewall, aiming to control e5.
d5 is a natural response, challenging our center. We don't mind—we'll build our wall with e3 next.
e3 prepares to develop the bishop to d3 and supports the pawn on d4. It also clears the way for f4, the signature Stonewall move.
Nf6 develops a piece and attacks our e4 square. We'll continue our plan, ignoring the knight for now.

Bd3 completes our Stonewall formation. The bishop is well-placed here, supporting the center and eyeing the kingside. Black's knight on f6 doesn't threaten anything yet, so we can calmly finish our setup. Next, we'll likely play f4 to solidify the pawn chain and prepare to clamp down on e5.
ideas.shortText: Bd3 finishes the Stonewall setup, eyeing the kingside.
